transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-17 16:00 UTC | Duration: 42m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (EdgeWork Head of ML), Tom Brooks (CTO), Elena Vasquez (Infra), Sam (SRE), Jing (Product)
Links shared: Redwood cost model (deck link), benchmark spreadsheet (google.com/sheet/abc - shorthand), internal infra diagram (edgework-private-vpc.png)

Auto-generated summary: discuss cost tradeoffs; customer wants clear cost per session and fallback behaviour.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, is this a good time?
[00:06] Priya Rao: Yep thanks, we only have about 40 minutes so we'll try to get into the cost bits early.
[00:11] Maya Chen: Perfect. Quick intros — I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, Liam is our SE.
[00:15] Liam O'Connor: Hi all, hey. Liam.
[00:18] Tom Brooks: Tom, CTO. Big question for us: we have a $60k/mo inference budget and need to figure out hosted vs dedicated vs put it in our VPC.
[00:27] Maya Chen: Great. That budget framing is super helpful. Priya — can you give a quick sense of latency requirements and expected QPS?
[00:35] Priya Rao: Sure. For our main conversational feature we need 99th percentile under 600ms for 512-token contexts. Peak qps around 60 concurrent active sessions but average is closer to 15. We also have an embedding pipeline for vector updates at off-peak times, that's lower priority.
[00:49] Liam O'Connor: OK, that mix suggests both low-latency tail requirements and some throughput bursts. Two levers we usually look at: batching windows to reduce per-token costs, and prefix/KV caching for repeated contexts — both move unit cost down but can affect tail latency.
[01:07] Priya Rao: Right, can you give ballpark numbers — like if we batch aggressively how much do we save on per-token?
[01:14] Liam O'Connor: Ballpark — depends on model size/quantization. For a 13B-ish open model running on optimized GPUs, batching and kernel-level optimizations can cut per-token compute cost by ~30-60% versus single-request execution. With KV cache for repeated prefixes you can get another 10-40% savings depending on your cache hit rate.
[01:34] Sam (SRE): When you say cache hit rate, what's realistic? We have a lot of dynamic prompts, but some system messages are identical.
[01:41] Liam O'Connor: In practice, if you have conversational system prompts and a set of few-shot examples that are consistent, a 30-50% effective token reduction on average is realistic for mid-frequency workloads. For pure exploratory queries it's lower.
[01:53] Priya Rao: How does hosted pricing reflect those savings? The per-token price we pay — is it a flat number or does Redwood adjust for batching/cache?
[02:01] Maya Chen: Hosted per-token list price is published; the effective per-token you pay on Hosted includes backend batching and auto-batching but we don't invoice differently per token for batching. We provide tooling (and the cost model we'll send) to show effective cost after typical batching/cache effects. Dedicated has different economics: you pay for reserved capacity (committed) which lowers per-token compute cost at scale but you take more fixed commit.
[02:24] Tom Brooks: So with our $60k/mo cap, is Dedicated even possible? Sounds like a big commit.
[02:29] Liam O'Connor: You might start Hosted for quick time to value and move to Dedicated once you settle traffic patterns. For example, for your scale, a small dedicated pool can bring per-token inference compute down 20-40% compared to hosted at heavy sustained qps, but you'd need a multi-month commit to realize the unit saving.
[02:46] Jing (Product): What about Private (VPC) — our security folks push for private control plane, does that cost a lot more?
[02:52] Maya Chen: Private adds platform fees + infra packaging, and sometimes additional integration cost for KMS/HSM. The unit compute costs can be similar to Dedicated if you self-host infra, but there are one-time setup fees and typically a support/enterprise license.
[03:06] Elena Vasquez: Our compliance folks require audit logs and on-prem options for some clients. Can Redwood deliver that in Private?
[03:11] Liam O'Connor: Yes — Private includes audit logs, SSO/SAML integrations, KMS options. We'll include the Private packaging breakdown in the docs.
[03:20] Priya Rao: Can we run a simple example? Say a 512-token request, using a 13B model. What is a rough per-response cost hosted vs dedicated?
[03:29] Liam O'Connor: Rough rule of thumb: hosted per-token compute + infra might map to $0.0008–$0.002 per token depending on model and optimizations. So a 512-token response could be $0.4–$1.0. With batching and cache that could drop to $0.2–$0.6 effective. Dedicated at scale can push that lower, maybe $0.15–$0.5 depending on commitment and quantization. These are rough — we'll send calibrated numbers.
[04:01] Tom Brooks: Those ranges are wide. What about quantization — can we run int8 or 4-bit in Redwood? How does that change cost?
[04:08] Liam O'Connor: Yes we support quantized model variants; int8/4-bit reduces memory and can increase throughput, typically improving unit cost by ~1.3x-2x depending on model and accuracy tradeoffs. There's also model quality variance; we can run side-by-side evals.
[04:23] Priya Rao: For our product the 99th-pctl tail is priority; we can't tolerate 1s+ spikes. How do batching windows not blow up tail latency?
[04:33] Liam O'Connor: Two common patterns: adaptive batching (small windows under low QPS, larger windows under high qps), and prioritized fast-paths for requests tagged latency-sensitive — they bypass batching or use smaller windows. Redwood's routing supports policy-based fast-path vs cost-path.
[04:51] Sam (SRE): Is that configurable per-route? We have a few routes that must be <600ms, others can be best-effort.
[04:57] Liam O'Connor: Yes, per-route configs: latency SLO, batching policy, fallback model. We'll demo that in the next call.
[05:05] Priya Rao: Any gotchas around warm KV caches and cold starts for our conversational workload?
[05:09] Liam O'Connor: Cold start latency is usually compute startup or model load; in Hosted we keep warmed pools to meet SLOs. With Dedicated you control pool sizing to avoid cold starts. Cache warming strategies (prefetch popular prefixes) help; we'll share a short playbook.
[05:22] Tom Brooks: On the budget math — if you show us a worked example how do we factor in 95th/99th tail?
[05:28] Maya Chen: Our cost model sheet will include multiple slices: median tokens per session, 95th and 99th token lengths, cache hit rates, batching window size, and a scenario comparator for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private with monthly cost and unit cost.
[05:41] Priya Rao: Can you also show break-even commit size for Dedicated? Like at what sustained qps/month do we save vs Hosted?
[05:48] Liam O'Connor: Yep, we'll calculate break-even given your traffic profile. For many customers the break-even is when you have consistent sustained load > certain hours/day; we'll compute that specifically.
[05:58] Jing (Product): One gotcha — we often have maintenance windows and blackouts. How do rolling deploys affect costs? If you have to reroute or fall back, do costs spike?
[06:07] Maya Chen: Failovers can temporarily increase cost if you route to higher-cost variants; Redwood supports automatic fallback to compatible model variants with policy controls. We'll show historical examples in the follow-up.
[06:17] Priya Rao: Security question — if we go Private and keep traffic in our VPC, do we still get Redwood's runtime optimizations like batching and kernel selection?
[06:26] Liam O'Connor: Yes — the runtime is included. Some kernel selection depends on hardware; for on-prem you choose supported GPUs and we tune for them.
[06:33] Sam (SRE): Can we run a quick pilot where Redwood runs a bench against our private staging VPC?
[06:38] Maya Chen: Absolutely — proposed next step: you share two workloads and a staging VPC endpoint; we schedule a 60-minute bench where we'll run both hosted-simulated and private runs and produce a cost rundown.
[06:50] Tom Brooks: Ok that sounds good. Pricing: do you have enterprise discounts or committed credits?
[06:55] Maya Chen: Yes committed capacity discounts apply for Dedicated and Private licensing; Hosted has volume tiers. We'll include proposed pricing ranges in the spreadsheet and a sample contract note.
[07:05] Priya Rao: Anything else we should consider?
[07:09] Liam O'Connor: Think about evaluation metrics: not just avg latency and cost but also perceived latency, percentiles, and failure modes. Also consider embedding/async workloads separately — those are cheaper and can be scheduled off-peak.
[07:23] Jing (Product): Can you attach a simple worked example in the doc for our 512-token use-case?
[07:28] Maya Chen: We'll do that.
